I would like to share a few constructive thoughts regarding the structure of our course. Instead of delivering direct lectures, our instructor encourages us to engage with the material by responding to questions and discussing content from the course reader. While this method can be intellectually stimulating, I believe that, especially when dealing with complex or unfamiliar topics, direct instruction from the professor could be significantly more beneficial for building a strong foundational understanding.

Additionally, the strict policy prohibiting the use of electronic devices such as tablets during class feels somewhat limiting. These tools can greatly enhance access to course materials and facilitate more efficient note-taking.

That being said, I want to emphasize that I have no personal issues with our instructor. On the contrary, I have great respect for their expertise and teaching. My intention is simply to offer these suggestions in the hope of contributing to a more effective and inclusive learning environment.

Professor Sorrell is a great teacher who helps us understand each subject from a creative and unique perspective. I appreciate the new insights he provides on historical texts; however, I believe his teaching methods could be more effective. Specifically, he tends to rush through each topic. For example, when we have a 25-page text to read, we often only discuss 4 to 5 paragraphs from random sections in class. This makes it difficult to grasp what he is discussing and what perspective he is trying to focus on. Recently, he introduced group presentations, where he divides the class into groups of 3 or 4 to teach on subjects chosen by him. While the idea is great, we do not get to choose our group members, which can result in being paired with individuals who may not contribute effectively, making cooperation very challenging. Additionally, I've noticed that despite reading and studying every text thoroughly, I received a much lower score than my classmates who relied on AI to study for the exams. This leads me to question whether all the reading is necessary if some can achieve higher grades with minimal effort in a single day. Regarding the exams, the format is creative and encourages new perspectives; however, Professor Sorrell did not clearly outline his expectations, which led to confusion about what was required in such thought-provoking exams. Overall, he is a great teacher.
